paras: The mobbing of William Batmun was an assault by a crowd on a Black man from Brooklyn at Coney Island, New York, in August 1900, after he escaped from an arresting officer. Police dispersed the crowd after it struck and kicked him, and he was fined $10 in police court. The episode is known from a single brief New York dispatch printed in a Wilmington, Delaware paper.

According to the dispatch, Batmun, of 57 Fleet place, Brooklyn, got drunk and insulted a woman on the Bowery at Coney Island and was arrested by Special Officer Summer. On the way to the station house, the dispatch said, he fired a .32-caliber revolver at the officer without effect and ran. A crowd overtook him, and he was struck on the head and kicked before Captain Driscoll and several central office detectives dispersed it. The size of the crowd and the extent of Batmun's injuries were not reported.

By the date of the dispatch, Aug. 20, Batmun had been fined $10 in the Coney Island police court. The coverage does not show any arrest of members of the crowd or any further charge over the revolver shot.

The Sun of Wilmington, Delaware, ran the story on Aug. 21 under the headline "Mobbed at Coney." as a short item datelined New York. The item identified Batmun as "a negro" and gave the police version of his conduct as fact, without comment on the crowd's beating. No report of the episode was found in New York papers or in the Black press.
